title: Tell It to Your Children
subtitle: Joel 1:1–14
description: A plague of locusts strips the land, and Joel's first command is to remember it and pass it on.
paragraphs: The book opens with a name and nothing else: “This is the word of the LORD that came to Joel son of Pethuel.” No king is named, no year is given, and nothing more is ever said about the man. What he was given to announce mattered more than when he announced it, and his first command is about memory. “Hear this, O elders; and give ear, all who dwell in the land. Has anything like this ever happened in your days or in the days of your fathers?” Then the instruction that outlives the plague itself: “Tell it to your children; let your children tell it to their children, and their children to the next generation.”

What they were to tell was a stripping, wave after wave of it. “What the devouring locust has left, the swarming locust has eaten; what the swarming locust has left, the young locust has eaten; and what the young locust has left, the destroying locust has eaten.” Four kinds of locust, each eating what the one before it left, until nothing remained for a fifth. Joel calls the swarm a nation and gives it a predator's mouth: “For a nation has invaded My land, powerful and without number; its teeth are the teeth of a lion, and its fangs are the fangs of a lioness.” The damage is described tree by tree: “It has laid waste My grapevine and splintered My fig tree. It has stripped off the bark and thrown it away; the branches have turned white.”

The mourning runs through every rank of the land. The drinkers are woken first: “Wake up, you drunkards, and weep,” because the sweet wine “has been cut off from your mouth.” A bride figure is called to grieve, wailing “like a virgin dressed in sackcloth, grieving for the husband of her youth.” Then the loss reaches the altar itself. “Grain and drink offerings have been cut off from the house of the LORD; the priests are in mourning, those who minister before the LORD.” With nothing left to harvest, there was nothing left to offer. Worship did not stop because the people lost heart. It stopped because the fields were empty.

The land itself is spoken to like a mourner. “The field is ruined; the land mourns. For the grain is destroyed, the new wine is dried up, and the oil fails.” The workers are named in their trades: “Be dismayed, O farmers, wail, O vinedressers, over the wheat and barley, because the harvest of the field has perished.” Tree after tree is listed in the withering, grapevine and fig, pomegranate, palm, and apple, until the summary lands on the people instead of the crops: “Surely the joy of mankind has dried up.”

Joel's answer to a stripped land is not an explanation. It is an assembly. The priests are told to dress for grief and stay in it: “Put on sackcloth and lament, O priests; wail, O ministers of the altar. Come, spend the night in sackcloth, O ministers of my God,” because the offerings “are withheld from the house of your God.” Then the call goes out to the whole population at once: “Consecrate a fast; proclaim a solemn assembly! Gather the elders and all the residents of the land to the house of the LORD your God, and cry out to the LORD.” When there is nothing left to bring God, the people are to bring themselves.

title: Alas for the Day
subtitle: Joel 1:15–2:11
description: The ruined fields become a preview of the Day of the LORD, and an army appears at dawn.
paragraphs: Midway through the mourning, Joel lifts his eyes from the ruined fields to something behind them. The plague is not the worst thing that has happened. It is a preview. “Alas for the day! For the Day of the LORD is near, and it will come as destruction from the Almighty.” The phrase will run through the whole book like a tolling bell. What the locusts did to one harvest in one land, that day will do on a scale no one can measure, and Joel wants the people to feel the nearness of it while they stand in the wreckage of the smaller one: “Has not the food been cut off before our very eyes,” along with “joy and gladness from the house of our God?”

The ruin is still underfoot as he speaks. “The seeds lie shriveled beneath the clods; the storehouses are in ruins; the granaries are broken down, for the grain has withered away.” Even the animals are drawn into the suffering, and Joel gives them a voice of their own: “How the cattle groan! The herds wander in confusion because they have no pasture. Even the flocks of sheep are suffering.” Beside the locusts has come fire and drought, pastures consumed and streams gone, until the whole created order around Judah is thirsty at once.

Then, for the only time in his book, the prophet steps out from behind the proclamation and prays in his own voice. “To You, O LORD, I call, for fire has consumed the open pastures and flames have scorched all the trees of the field.” He does not pray for himself. He prays the land's prayer, and he gives the animals a share in it: “Even the beasts of the field pant for You, for the streams of water have dried up, and fire has consumed the open pastures.” The man who announced the coming day is found on his knees inside the present one.

The trumpet answers him. “Blow the ram’s horn in Zion; sound the alarm on My holy mountain! Let all who dwell in the land tremble, for the Day of the LORD is coming; indeed, it is near.” What approaches is described as an army appearing at sunrise: “a day of darkness and gloom, a day of clouds and blackness. Like the dawn overspreading the mountains a great and strong army appears, such as never was of old, nor will ever be in ages to come.” Fire runs before and behind it. “The land before them is like the Garden of Eden, but behind them, it is like a desert wasteland.” The locusts of chapter 1 have grown into something the whole earth can see coming.

The charge is painted stroke by stroke. “Their appearance is like that of horses, and they gallop like swift steeds,” with “a sound like that of chariots” bounding over the mountaintops. They keep ranks no human army keeps, never jostling, never breaking formation, and no wall stops them: “They storm the city; they run along the wall; they climb into houses, entering through windows like thieves.” Before them “the earth quakes; the heavens tremble. The sun and moon grow dark, and the stars lose their brightness.” And the most frightening line is saved for last. The army has a commander. “The LORD raises His voice in the presence of His army. Indeed, His camp is very large, for mighty are those who obey His command. For the Day of the LORD is great and very dreadful. Who can endure it?” Joel leaves the question hanging in the air, unanswered.

title: Rend Your Hearts
subtitle: Joel 2:12–17
description: Yet even now: the LORD calls His people to return with all their heart.
paragraphs: The army has been described. The day is great and very dreadful, and the prophet has just asked who can endure it. The next two words are the hinge the whole book swings on: “Yet even now,” declares the LORD, “return to Me with all your heart, with fasting, weeping, and mourning.” Even now, with the trumpet already sounded and the horizon already dark, the door stands open. The call is not to survive the day but to return before it, and the terms are not distance or payment. The terms are the whole heart, brought back with fasting and tears.

The verse that follows is the most quoted line in Joel, and it draws a line between the outside and the inside of grief. “So rend your hearts and not your garments, and return to the LORD your God.” Torn clothing was the public sign of mourning, and God asks for the tearing to happen somewhere no one can see. The reason is His own character, stated in words Israel had heard since Sinai: “For He is gracious and compassionate, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. And He relents from sending disaster.” Repentance here is not a bet that a harsh God might soften. It is a return to a God whose described nature already leans toward mercy.

Joel does not promise the people a guaranteed outcome, and the honesty of that is part of the summons. “Who knows? He may turn and relent and leave a blessing behind Him,” and the blessing is named in the very currency the locusts destroyed: “grain and drink offerings for the LORD your God.” The stripped altar could be supplied again. The stripped fields could give something to bring. The people are asked to return without holding a contract, trusting that the God who relents from disaster is the kind of God who leaves blessings behind Him when He turns.

So the trumpet blows a second time in Zion, and this time it does not announce an army. “Blow the ram’s horn in Zion, consecrate a fast, proclaim a sacred assembly.” The gathering is total in a way the first fast only began. “Gather the people, sanctify the congregation, assemble the aged, gather the children, even those nursing at the breast.” No one is too old, no one is too young, and the exemptions that ordinary life allows are cancelled one by one, down to the most protected day a couple ever has.

“Let the bridegroom leave his room, and the bride her chamber.” Even a wedding gives way to this assembly. Then the book ends its summons at the place where heaven and earth meet in the temple, with the priests standing in the narrow space between the portico and the altar, weeping as they minister. Joel writes their prayer for them, and it is not a prayer about crops. “Spare Your people, O LORD, and do not make Your heritage a reproach, an object of scorn among the nations.” Underneath the plea for the harvest sits a plea for God's own name among the watching peoples: “Why should they say among the peoples, ‘Where is their God?’” The episode leaves the priests there, mid prayer, with the answer still to come.

title: I Will Repay the Years
subtitle: Joel 2:18–32
description: The LORD spares His people, restores the land, and promises to pour out His Spirit on all people.
paragraphs: The answer comes, and it begins inside God before it reaches the fields. “Then the LORD became jealous for His land, and He spared His people.” The plea the priests were told to pray, spare Your people, is answered in the same words. What follows is a reversal inventory, item for item against the losses of the plague. The offerings that failed are answered with supply: “Behold, I will send you grain, new wine, and oil, and by them you will be satisfied. I will never again make you a reproach among the nations.” The scorn the priests feared is named and cancelled by God Himself.

The invader is dealt with next, and no identity is given to it beyond its direction. “The northern army I will drive away from you, banishing it to a barren and desolate land, its front ranks into the Eastern Sea, and its rear guard into the Western Sea.” What marched in perfect formation will be scattered to both seas and left to rot in a wasteland, its stench rising where its terror had been. Then the fear commands of chapter 1 are reversed one by one, spoken now to the very creatures who mourned. “Do not be afraid, O land; rejoice and be glad, for the LORD has done great things.” “Do not be afraid, O beasts of the field, for the open pastures have turned green, the trees bear their fruit, and the fig tree and vine yield their best.”

The rain that Joel prayed over returns as a gift with a meaning attached. “Be glad, O children of Zion, and rejoice in the LORD your God, for He has given you the autumn rains for your vindication. He sends you showers, both autumn and spring rains, as before.” The harvest follows in the old abundance: “The threshing floors will be full of grain, and the vats will overflow with new wine and oil.” Then comes the promise that has carried this book into more sermons and songs than any other line in it: “I will repay you for the years eaten by locusts.” The devourers are named in a roll call, “the swarming locust, the young locust, the destroying locust, and the devouring locust,” and claimed as God's own instrument all along: “My great army that I sent against you.” Lost years, not just lost crops, are put on God's ledger to repay.

The restoration ends in knowledge and the end of shame. “You will have plenty to eat, until you are satisfied. You will praise the name of the LORD your God, who has worked wonders for you. My people will never again be put to shame.” Twice the sentence is sworn, here and again at the paragraph's end: “Then you will know that I am present in Israel and that I am the LORD your God, and there is no other. My people will never again be put to shame.” The God who seemed absent enough for nations to mock is present in the middle of His people, and He says so in the first person.

Then the horizon tears open past anything a harvest could mean. “And afterward, I will pour out My Spirit on all people. Your sons and daughters will prophesy, your old men will dream dreams, your young men will see visions.” The gift is not rationed by age, by sex, or by station: “Even on My menservants and maidservants, I will pour out My Spirit in those days.” Wonders follow in the heavens and on the earth, “blood and fire and columns of smoke,” and the sky itself darkens: “The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood before the coming of the great and awesome Day of the LORD.” But the last word of the promise is an open door, fenced by nothing: “And everyone who calls on the name of the LORD will be saved; for on Mount Zion and in Jerusalem there will be deliverance, as the LORD has promised, among the remnant called by the LORD.”

title: Multitudes in the Valley of Decision
subtitle: Joel 3:1–21
description: The nations are gathered for judgment, and the book ends with the LORD dwelling in Zion.
paragraphs: The last chapter looks past the harvest to the settling of every account. “Yes, in those days and at that time, when I restore Judah and Jerusalem from captivity, I will gather all the nations and bring them down to the Valley of Jehoshaphat.” The valley is named for what happens there, since Jehoshaphat means the LORD judges, and no location is given for it anywhere in the book. The charges are read out like a court record. “There I will enter into judgment against them concerning My people, My inheritance, Israel, whom they have scattered among the nations as they divided up My land.” Then the smallest and cruelest items on the list: “They cast lots for My people; they bartered a boy for a prostitute and sold a girl for wine to drink.” Children were treated as currency, and heaven kept the receipts.

Tyre, Sidon, and the regions of Philistia are addressed by name, as traders who profited from Judah's fall. “For you took My silver and gold and carried off My finest treasures to your temples. You sold the people of Judah and Jerusalem to the Greeks, to send them far from their homeland.” The sentence mirrors the crime with a precision the traders cannot miss: “Behold, I will rouse them from the places to which you sold them; I will return your recompense upon your heads.” Their own sons and daughters will be sold into the hands of Judah, and on-sold to the Sabeans, “to a distant nation.” The people who shipped Judah's children far from home will watch their own sent just as far. “Indeed, the LORD has spoken.”

Then the summons goes out, and it is a war summons thrown back at the nations in their own language. “Proclaim this among the nations”: “Prepare for war; rouse the mighty men; let all the men of war advance and attack!” The most famous peace promise in the prophets is turned inside out, deliberately: “Beat your plowshares into swords and your pruning hooks into spears. Let the weak say, ‘I am strong!’” Where Isaiah and Micah saw farm tools made from weapons when God's reign came in peace, Joel's valley demands weapons made from farm tools, because the nations are being gathered for judgment, not for a festival. Even the prophet joins the cry: “Bring down Your mighty ones, O LORD.”

The judgment itself is pictured as a harvest, the dark twin of the overflowing vats in the restoration. “Let the nations be roused and advance to the Valley of Jehoshaphat, for there I will sit down to judge all the nations on every side.” Then the commands fall like blows: “Swing the sickle, for the harvest is ripe. Come, trample the grapes, for the winepress is full; the wine vats overflow because their wickedness is great.” The crowd in the valley gets the line the whole book is remembered by: “Multitudes, multitudes in the valley of decision! For the Day of the LORD is near in the valley of decision.” The lights go out over the scene as before, sun and moon dark and stars gone, and then the voice: “The LORD will roar from Zion and raise His voice from Jerusalem; heaven and earth will tremble. But the LORD will be a refuge for His people, a stronghold for the people of Israel.”

The book closes with the land healed and the account of blood settled. “Then you will know that I am the LORD your God, who dwells in Zion, My holy mountain. Jerusalem will be holy, never again to be overrun by foreigners.” Blessing pours downhill in every direction: “the mountains will drip with sweet wine, and the hills will flow with milk,” every stream in Judah running with water, “and a spring will flow from the house of the LORD to water the Valley of Acacias.” Against that picture stand two names: “Egypt will become desolate, and Edom a desert wasteland, because of the violence done to the people of Judah, in whose land they shed innocent blood.” Judah, by contrast, endures: “But Judah will be inhabited forever, and Jerusalem from generation to generation.” And the smallest book of prophecy ends where it was always heading, not with a date or a battle but with a dwelling: “For the LORD dwells in Zion.”
